\begin{abstract}
Latent world models plan by ranking action-conditioned rollouts
according to their terminal distance from an encoded visual goal. In
the official LeWM setup, five-step action blocks and a five-block CEM
plan give a planning span of $H{=}25$ environment steps. When the goal
offset $o$ exceeds this span, the terminal cost compares
representations associated with different future times, creating a
temporal mismatch between short-term prediction and long-horizon
progress. We identify this mismatch as a critical bottleneck in
terminal latent scoring and introduce Horizon-Aligned Scoring (HAS).
HAS trains an action-free Forward imaginer on local latent
transitions, then recursively propagates each short-rollout endpoint
across the remaining temporal gap before computing its goal distance.
This extends the scoring horizon without requiring action-conditioned
prediction over the full goal offset. Across ten paired evaluation
groups on PushT, TwoRoom, and Reacher, HAS improves success at every
tested offset beyond $H$. It raises PushT success from $42.8\%$ to
$67.8\%$ at goal offset $o{=}50$ and TwoRoom success from $16.4\%$ to
$70.4\%$ at $o{=}100$. HAS also outperforms Long-CEM, a LeWM planner
with span $H{=}50$, at all long offsets, showing that aligning the
scoring horizon can be more effective than lengthening the
action-conditioned rollout.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Learning a world model from reward-free trajectories provides a route to
goal-conditioned control without a task-specific policy. The model
encodes observations, predicts how candidate actions change their latent
representations, and plans directly against an encoded goal
image~\citep{sobal2025rewardfree,zhou2025dinowm,lewm2026}. This
prediction-based interface is useful when goals are specified visually
or change after training. Its planning quality, however, depends on both
the latent dynamics and the criterion used to rank predicted outcomes.

LeWorldModel (LeWM)~\citep{lewm2026} learns compact visual dynamics with
an end-to-end Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture
(JEPA)~\citep{lecun2022jepa}. At test time, the Cross-Entropy Method
(CEM)~\citep{rubinstein1999cem} samples action sequences, rolls the
predictor forward for a fixed horizon, and minimizes Euclidean distance
between the predicted endpoint and the goal embedding. We adopt the
official LeWM temporal discretization: $b{=}5$ environment actions form
one action block, CEM optimizes $h{=}5$ blocks, and the planning span
is $H{=}hb{=}25$ environment steps.

A goal may refer to an observation farther than $H$ steps into the
future. The planner must then use a short candidate rollout to make
progress toward a goal that remains beyond its planning span.
Direct terminal distance compares representations with different
temporal roles: the candidate endpoint describes where the agent could
be after the current plan, whereas the goal describes where it should be
after additional action blocks. The score therefore conflates the
quality of the current action sequence with the unmodeled temporal gap
between its endpoint and the goal. We call this comparison
\emph{temporal mismatch}. It identifies a concrete ambiguity in
terminal scoring; other sources of error, including inaccurate dynamics
and poorly structured latent distances, may remain.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_has_evaluation.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Evaluation-time horizon alignment.}
\textbf{Top:} LeWM evaluates the endpoint of an action-conditioned
rollout directly against the encoded goal.
\textbf{Bottom:} HAS applies the action-free Forward imaginer after the
short rollout and compares the resulting horizon-aligned
representation with the goal. The lower rows illustrate how alignment
is recomputed after successive replanning steps.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure}

Horizon-Aligned Scoring (HAS) resolves this ambiguity by constructing a
representation at the goal horizon for every candidate
(Figure~\ref{fig:overview}). A deterministic, action-free Forward
imaginer $F$ learns to advance LeWM latents by one action block. The
imaginer receives detached predictor outputs and is supervised by later
encoder latents with one-step and recursive two-step losses. During
planning, the action-conditioned predictor first produces the
$H$-step endpoint of each candidate. HAS then applies $F$ once for
each remaining action block and computes the ordinary goal distance
from the resulting horizon-aligned endpoint. Replanning reduces the
number of Forward steps as execution advances.

Our evaluation isolates the effect of this scoring rule across four
goal offsets on PushT, TwoRoom, and Reacher. When $o{=}H{=}25$, HAS
uses $k{=}0$ and matches LeWM within evaluation variation. At every
tested offset beyond $H$, HAS raises mean success. The largest gains
are $25.0$ points on PushT at $o{=}50$ and $56.2$ points on TwoRoom at
$o{=}75$. Long-CEM, a LeWM planner with span $H{=}50$, remains below
HAS at all long offsets on all three tasks. These results support
horizon alignment as a useful scoring operation in the tested LeWM
setting. Prediction and representation errors remain separate sources
of planning error.

The paper makes three contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item We formulate long-offset terminal scoring as a temporal
correspondence problem between a short-rollout endpoint and a later
goal.
\item We introduce HAS, a scoring method that trains an action-free
Forward imaginer with detached one-step and recursive supervision, then
uses it to align candidate endpoints with the goal time.
\item We evaluate HAS over ten paired evaluation groups on three visual
control tasks, including a Long-CEM control with span $H{=}50$, and
find consistent gains beyond the default planning span $H{=}25$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Planning with latent dynamics.}
Model-based control commonly evaluates candidate actions through
predicted future states~\citep{hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer,
hansen2022tdmpc}. Reconstruction-free approaches instead learn and plan
in a representation space. PLDM trains JEPA dynamics from reward-free
offline data and uses latent planning for visual goal
reaching~\citep{sobal2025rewardfree}. DINO-WM builds dynamics over
pre-trained visual features~\citep{zhou2025dinowm}, while LeWM learns
its encoder and predictor end-to-end with prediction and distributional
regularization~\citep{lewm2026}. These planners rank actions with
terminal latent distance. HAS studies the case in which the endpoint
used by that distance covers less time than the goal offset.

\paragraph{Extending the planning horizon.}
One line of work increases temporal reach within the world model or the
search procedure. VLWM trains action-conditioned prediction over
variable-length action chunks~\citep{du2026vlwm}. Hierarchical World
Models predict at multiple temporal resolutions and use coarse outcomes
to guide lower-level planning~\citep{zhang2026hwm}. FF-JEPA predicts
latent subgoals with an action-free model before solving each local
control problem~\citep{masip2026ffjepa}, and SAGE conditions candidate
action generation on predicted subgoals~\citep{cheng2026sage}. HAS
does not use its Forward imaginer to specify an intermediate target or
to generate actions. It applies the imaginer after an
action-conditioned candidate rollout so that terminal comparisons refer
to the goal time.

\paragraph{Planning-oriented representations and costs.}
Prediction accuracy alone need not produce representations that rank
actions well. RC-aux adds reward-consistency objectives to shape latent
models for downstream planning~\citep{li2026rcaux}. Temporal
straightening regularizes trajectories so Euclidean displacement better
reflects temporal and geodesic structure~\citep{wang2026straightening}.
Traj-LeWM jointly learns a goal-conditioned latent trajectory cost and
combines it with endpoint distance~\citep{huang2026trajlewm}. These
methods alter representation learning or introduce trajectory-level
task signals. HAS instead learns a local, goal-agnostic temporal map
from the same observation sequences used to train the world model.

\paragraph{Reachability-aware terminal scoring.}
Trajectory Reachability Metrics (TRM) train a pairwise head on
horizon-matched temporal separations and use its scalar output as a
replacement or hybrid terminal cost~\citep{li2026trm}. TRM addresses
whether latent proximity reflects reachability. HAS addresses which
time-indexed representation should enter the proximity calculation. The
two methods therefore intervene at different parts of the scoring
interface: TRM learns a new comparison, whereas HAS advances a candidate
endpoint to the goal horizon before applying latent distance.

\section{Background and problem setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Goal-conditioned latent control.}
Let $x_t$ denote an image observation and $u_t$ an environment action at
time $t$. The encoder maps an image to
$z_t=E(x_t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Training and planning group
$b=5$ consecutive environment actions into an action block
$a_j=(u_{bj},\ldots,u_{bj+b-1})$. A transition in latent time therefore
represents $b$ environment steps. Given recent latents and action
blocks, the action-conditioned predictor $P$ estimates the next latent.

At evaluation, a goal image $x_g=x_{\tau+o}$ is sampled at goal offset
$o$ from the initial observation $x_\tau$, and
$z_g=E(x_g)$. At a replanning step, $e$ environment steps have elapsed
since $x_\tau$. CEM considers candidate sequences of $h{=}5$ action
blocks, giving planning span $H{=}hb{=}25$ environment steps. For
candidate $a^{(n)}_{0:h-1}$, autoregressive prediction yields endpoint
\begin{equation}
\hat z^{(n)}_{e+H}
=P^{(h)}(z_e,a^{(n)}_{0:h-1}).
\label{eq:predict-endpoint}
\end{equation}
LeWM ranks the candidate by
\begin{equation}
C_{\mathrm{LeWM}}^{(n)}
=\left\|\hat z^{(n)}_{e+H}-z_g\right\|_2^2.
\label{eq:lewm-cost}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Temporal mismatch.}
When $o-e>H$, the two arguments in
Equation~\ref{eq:lewm-cost} refer to different future times. The
predicted endpoint is indexed by $e+H$, while the goal is indexed by
$o$. Their temporal gap is $o-e-H$. Consequently, the terminal score
mixes two quantities: progress induced by the current candidate and the
remaining evolution after that candidate ends. HAS recursively advances
each endpoint for the number of action blocks separating $e+H$ from
$o$, then computes the goal distance. This operation makes the temporal
correspondence explicit. Accurate dynamics and a planning-relevant
latent geometry remain necessary.

\section{Horizon-aligned scoring}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{LeWM training interface}
\label{sec:lewm}

Each training sample contains four encoded observations
$z_{0:3}=E(x_{0:3})$ separated by one action block. With zero-based
indices, LeWM produces predictions $p_{0:2}$ such that
$p_i$ predicts $z_{i+1}$. Its world-model objective is
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LeWM}}
=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{i=0}^{2}\|p_i-z_{i+1}\|_2^2
+0.09\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}}(z_{0:3}),
\label{eq:lewm}
\end{equation}
where SIGReg encourages non-collapsed, approximately isotropic latent
representations~\citep{lewm2026}. The encoder targets are not
stop-gradient targets in this objective.

\subsection{Action-free Forward imaginer}
\label{sec:imaginer}

HAS introduces a map $F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}$ that
advances a latent by one action block without receiving the intervening
actions. $F$ is deterministic. It contains two residual MLP blocks, each
using LayerNorm, a $192\!\rightarrow\!768\!\rightarrow\!192$ projection,
and GELU activation, followed by output normalization and a linear
projection. Its action-free input makes $F$ a marginal predictor of
local latent evolution in the offline trajectories, rather than a model
of candidate-specific dynamics.

Training uses the alignment $p_i\approx z_{i+1}$ supplied by LeWM.
Inputs and targets for $F$ are detached from both $P$ and $E$; bars
denote this detachment below. Two local transitions supervise
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{step}}
=\frac{1}{2}\left(
\|F(\bar p_0)-\bar z_2\|_2^2+
\|F(\bar p_1)-\bar z_3\|_2^2\right).
\label{eq:forward-step}
\end{equation}
A recursive term additionally supervises the composition used at test
time:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}
=\|F(F(\bar p_0))-\bar z_3\|_2^2.
\label{eq:forward-roll}
\end{equation}
The legacy Forward objective is
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{F}
=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{step}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}.
\label{eq:forward-total}
\end{equation}
The Forward objective enters training with unit weight. Detachment
confines its gradients to $F$, while $E$ and $P$ continue to receive the
LeWM objective. Figure~\ref{fig:method} contrasts the LeWM prediction
objective with the detached supervision used to train $F$.
Appendix~\ref{app:implementation} documents an additional
parameter-disjoint training head present in the reported checkpoints.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_has_training.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{LeWM and Forward training pipelines.}
\textbf{Top:} the official LeWM pipeline jointly trains the encoder and
action-conditioned causal predictor.
\textbf{Bottom:} the Forward-augmented pipeline adds an action-free
causal imaginer trained from subsequent latent targets. The detailed
step and recursive objectives are given in
Equations~\ref{eq:forward-step}--\ref{eq:forward-total}.}
\label{fig:method}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Dynamic horizon alignment}
\label{sec:alignment}

At elapsed time $e$, the temporal gap after the candidate rollout is
$o-e-H$. Because one application of $F$ represents one $b$-step action
block, HAS uses recursion depth
\begin{equation}
k(e,o)=\max\left(\frac{o-e-H}{b},\,0\right).
\label{eq:depth}
\end{equation}
The evaluated offsets and replanning times are chosen so that the
positive numerator is divisible by $b$. Starting from the
action-conditioned endpoint, define
$F^0(z)=z$ and $F^{j+1}(z)=F(F^j(z))$. HAS ranks candidate $n$ by
\begin{equation}
C_{\mathrm{HAS}}^{(n)}
=\left\|F^{k(e,o)}\!\left(\hat z^{(n)}_{e+H}\right)-z_g\right\|_2^2.
\label{eq:has-cost}
\end{equation}
The Forward trajectory after $\hat z^{(n)}_{e+H}$ is action-free. It
does not prescribe the future controls that lead to the imagined state;
its role is to provide a time-aligned representation for ranking the
current action-conditioned candidates.

\subsection{Receding-horizon planning}
\label{sec:planning}

At each replanning step, CEM optimizes a diagonal Gaussian distribution
over $h$ action blocks using Algorithm~\ref{alg:has-cem}. Each iteration
evaluates $N$ candidates, retains the $M$ candidates with lowest HAS
cost, and fits the next distribution to their empirical moments. The
solver returns the final mean action sequence. The controller executes
its receding-horizon prefix, updates $e$, and repeats the procedure from
the new observation.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Horizon-Aligned CEM at elapsed time $e$}
\label{alg:has-cem}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require current latent $z_e$; goal latent $z_g$; goal offset $o$
\Require predictor $P$; Forward imaginer $F$; block size $b$; span $H=hb$
\Require candidates $N$; elites $M$; CEM iterations $J$
\Ensure optimized action-block sequence $A^\star$
\State $k \gets \max\!\left((o-e-H)/b,\,0\right)$
\State $(\mu_0,\sigma_0) \gets \Call{InitializeCEM}{h}$
\For{$j=1,\ldots,J$}
    \State $A^{(1:N)}
        \gets \Call{Sample}{\mu_{j-1},\sigma_{j-1},N}$
    \ForAll{$n\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$}
        \State $\hat z^{(n)}_{e+H}
            \gets P^{(h)}(z_e,A^{(n)})$
        \State $\tilde z^{(n)}_{o}
            \gets F^{k}(\hat z^{(n)}_{e+H})$
        \State $c_n \gets \|\tilde z^{(n)}_{o}-z_g\|_2^2$
    \EndFor
    \State $\mathcal{I}_j \gets \Call{Elite}{c_{1:N},M}$
    \State $(\mu_j,\sigma_j)
        \gets \Call{Moments}{\{A^{(n)}:n\in\mathcal{I}_j\}}$
\EndFor
\State \Return $A^\star\gets\mu_J$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

The depth is recomputed after every executed plan. When $o{=}H$,
$k{=}0$ and HAS reduces to the LeWM cost. For a goal offset $o{=}100$
and default span $H{=}25$, successive replans use depths $15$, $10$,
$5$, and $0$ at elapsed times $0$, $25$, $50$, and $75$.

HAS adds $k$ evaluations of a small residual MLP for every candidate.
Its additional computational cost grows linearly with both the Forward
depth and the number of sampled candidates; the depth decreases to zero
as the goal horizon is approached.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:exp}

\subsection{Evaluation protocol}

We evaluate LeWM, HAS, and Long-CEM on
PushT~\citep{florence2022ibc}, TwoRoom~\citep{sobal2025rewardfree}, and
Reacher~\citep{lewm2026} using one epoch-$10$ training checkpoint per
task. Ten
evaluation groups, seeds $42$--$51$, each provide $50$ episodes. Within
a task and group, all planner configurations share the same starts.
These groups measure start-sampling and CEM variability; they are not
independent training seeds. We report the mean and standard deviation
of the ten group-level success rates, together with paired
group-bootstrap $95\%$ intervals on HAS$-$baseline gaps.

Goal offsets are $o\in\{25,50,75,100\}$ environment steps, following
the official LeWM multi-offset sweep. The interaction budget is
$2o$. LeWM and HAS use $h{=}5$ action blocks, so $H{=}25$ and HAS
uses $k{=}0$ exactly when $o{=}H$. Long-CEM is a LeWM planner with
$h{=}10$ blocks and receding horizon $10$, giving span $H{=}50$. At
$o{=}25$, this plan extends beyond the goal time; we report the
condition for completeness and treat $o\ge 50$ as the relevant
longer-horizon control. All configurations use $b{=}5$, $300$
candidates, $30$ elites, and $30$ CEM updates. We use the success
criterion defined by each environment.

\subsection{Main results}
\label{sec:main}

HAS matches LeWM at $o{=}H{=}25$ and improves mean success at every
larger offset (Figure~\ref{fig:multiseed}, Table~\ref{tab:main}). On
PushT the paired gaps are $+25.0$ points at $o{=}50$
($95\%$ CI $[20.6,28.8]$), $+18.8$ at $o{=}75$, and $+10.2$ at
$o{=}100$, each with HAS ahead on all ten groups. On TwoRoom the
corresponding gaps are $+38.0$, $+56.2$, and $+54.0$ points, again
with ten-for-ten group wins. Reacher is already a high-success LeWM
setting; HAS still adds $+3.4$, $+9.2$, and $+9.8$ points at
$o\in\{50,75,100\}$, with no group loss.

Long-CEM does not reproduce these gains. At $o\ge 50$, HAS exceeds
Long-CEM by $28.0$, $20.6$, and $8.4$ points on PushT, by $25.8$,
$48.4$, and $47.4$ points on TwoRoom, and by $18.0$, $8.4$, and
$7.4$ points on Reacher. The $o{=}25$ Long-CEM column is weaker still
on PushT and Reacher, consistent with executing a $50$-step plan
toward a $25$-step goal. Lengthening the action-conditioned rollout
is therefore not a substitute for aligning the scoring time.

\subsection{Analysis and mechanism}
\label{sec:analysis}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_has_process.pdf}
\caption{Executed frames on one shared start per task. Columns are
environment steps in increments of the action block $b{=}5$, plus the
visual goal. All three tasks use $o{=}75$. LeWM ($H{=}25$) fails on
these starts; HAS reaches the goal. The strips are qualitative
examples, not additional quantitative results.}
\label{fig:process}
\end{figure*}

The long-offset gap is visible in execution, not only in aggregate
rates. Figure~\ref{fig:process} shows one shared start on PushT,
TwoRoom, and Reacher. LeWM does not reach the goal. HAS does. The
examples illustrate the paired contrast below; they are not additional
quantitative results.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_has_paired_delta.pdf}
\caption{Paired success gaps (percentage points) with
group-bootstrap $95\%$ intervals. Blue compares HAS with LeWM at
$H{=}25$; teal compares HAS with Long-CEM at $H{=}50$. The
$o{=}25$ teal bars are the Long-CEM overshoot condition.}
\label{fig:paired}
\end{figure}

If temporal mismatch is the operative error, two consequences should
hold. First, HAS and LeWM should coincide whenever $k{=}0$. They do:
TwoRoom and Reacher match exactly at $o{=}25$, and PushT differs by
$-0.2$ points (CI $[-0.8,0.4]$). Second, the gain should appear only
after $o>H$ and should survive a longer action-conditioned baseline.
Figure~\ref{fig:paired} shows both patterns. The $k{=}0$ column is an
internal ranking control: the same CEM candidates and the same
terminal metric produce the same decisions when no Forward steps are
applied.

The Forward map itself moves latents as depth increases. Across the
ten groups, $\|F^{k}(z)-z\|_2$ rises from $1.06$ to $1.26$ on PushT,
from $0.90$ to $1.08$ on Reacher, and remains near $1.00$ on TwoRoom
for $k\in\{1,5,10,15\}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:analysis}). TwoRoom
therefore does not need large Euclidean travel to change candidate
order; the same recursion that barely displaces the seed latent still
restores long-offset success. This is consistent with HAS as a
time-alignment operator rather than a reconstruction of the full
future observation.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_has_latents.pdf}
\caption{Held-out latent geometry, excluding evaluation-manifest
episodes. Top: PCA of the action-conditioned time $z_{t+25}$, the
HAS-aligned point $F^{10}(z_{t+25})$, and the encoded goal
$z_{t+75}$. Bottom: temporal retrieval accuracy of $F^{k}(z_t)$
against encoder latents at $t{+}5j$. The scatter is a visualization;
the retrieval curve is the quantitative check. These panels do not
claim $F^{k}(z)=z_{t+kb}$.}
\label{fig:latents}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:latents} examines the same map on held-out dataset
windows rather than CEM candidates. PCA places $F^{10}(z_{t+25})$
relative to $z_{t+25}$ and $z_{t+75}$; t-SNE and goal-distance
histograms are in Appendix~\ref{app:analysis}. Retrieval accuracy
asks whether $F^{k}(z_t)$ is nearest the encoder latent at
$t{+}5k$. A TwoRoom cloud that remains compact is compatible with
the near-unit displacement already reported: a small Euclidean move
can still change the nearest future time.

HAS also does not buy its gains with a longer predictor rollout.
Table~\ref{tab:cost} reports wall-clock seconds per $50$-episode
group. At $o{=}25$, HAS and LeWM take essentially the same time, while
Long-CEM is $1.3$--$1.6\times$ slower. At $o{=}100$, HAS remains
comparable to LeWM on PushT and Reacher and is faster on TwoRoom,
where earlier successes shorten executed episodes. The additional
cost of $F$ is therefore small relative to doubling the
action-conditioned span.

\subsection{Ablations}
\label{sec:ablation}

The protocol already isolates the two design questions that matter
most. Alignment depth is tested by $o{=}25$, where $k{=}0$ disables
$F$ and HAS reduces to LeWM. The same scoring rule, with $k>0$, is
what produces the $o>H$ gains. Extra action-conditioned compute is
tested by Long-CEM: increasing $H$ from $25$ to $50$ does not match
HAS at $o\ge 50$ and is strictly worse at the $o{=}25$ overshoot.

Table~\ref{tab:kdepth} holds the Forward checkpoint fixed and replaces
the dynamic schedule with a constant depth on the seed-$42$ starts.
$k{=}0$ should recover LeWM. $k{=}5$ under-aligns a $75$- or
$100$-step goal; $k{=}15$ overshoots the $o{=}75$ schedule
($k{=}10$ at the first replan).

A single-group PushT check further supports the action-free
assumption. An action-aligned Forward and a sequential
action-conditioned Forward, trained and evaluated on the same seed-$42$
starts, reach $58\%$ and $68\%$ at $o{=}50$ versus $62\%$ for the
reported action-free HAS run, and both fall behind at $o{=}75$ and
$o{=}100$ (Appendix~\ref{app:ablation}). Conditioning $F$ on predicted
actions is therefore not required for the mid-range gain, and it does
not improve the long-offset setting in this protocol. The reported
models use the joint $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{step}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}$
objective; we do not claim a full step-versus-roll training sweep.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}

Each task uses one training checkpoint. The ten evaluation groups
quantify start and planner variability, not training-seed variability.
Long-CEM is one alternative span and is not compute-matched to HAS.
PushT success is still $23.4\%$ at $o{=}100$. HAS assumes that the
temporal goal offset is available when selecting $k$.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:concl}

This paper examines terminal scoring when a latent world model predicts
over a shorter interval than the offset of a visual goal. Direct
endpoint-to-goal distance then compares representations associated with
different future times. HAS makes this temporal correspondence explicit:
an action-free Forward imaginer advances each action-conditioned
endpoint by the remaining number of action blocks before the goal
distance is evaluated.

Across ten paired evaluation groups, HAS improves success over LeWM at
every tested offset beyond the default span $H{=}25$ on PushT,
TwoRoom, and Reacher. The gains are largest at $o{=}50$ on PushT and
$o{=}75$ on TwoRoom, while PushT at $o{=}100$ remains difficult.
Long-CEM, with span $H{=}50$, does not match HAS. The $k{=}0$
identity at $o{=}H$ and the failure of a longer action-conditioned
rollout support horizon alignment as the operative change. The
evidence remains specific to one checkpoint per task. HAS also requires
the goal offset to set its recursion depth, and comparisons against
learned terminal metrics remain incomplete.

\section{Training and implementation details}
\label{app:implementation}

\paragraph{Time indexing.}
The dataset loader returns four observations separated by a frame skip
of five environment steps. The three prediction outputs are indexed
$p_0,p_1,p_2$ and align with encoder latents $z_1,z_2,z_3$,
respectively. The legacy Forward variant receives $p_0$ and $p_1$ as
its one-step inputs, with $z_2$ and $z_3$ as targets. Its recursive
example starts from $p_0$ and targets $z_3$ after two applications.
Thus every supervised or imagined Forward transition corresponds to one
five-step action block.

\paragraph{Architecture and gradients.}
The Forward imaginer operates on $192$-dimensional latents. Each of its
two residual blocks applies LayerNorm, a linear expansion to width
$768$, GELU, and a linear projection to width $192$ before the residual
addition. A final LayerNorm and $192$-dimensional linear projection
produce the output. Predictor inputs and encoder targets are detached
before all Forward computations. Consequently,
$\mathcal{L}_{F}$ updates only the Forward parameters.

\paragraph{Optimization.}
The reported models use AdamW with learning rate $5\times10^{-5}$ and
weight decay $10^{-3}$, batch size $128$, bfloat16 training, and
gradient clipping at norm $1.0$. The LeWM SIGReg coefficient is $0.09$.
The Forward step and recursive terms each have coefficient $1.0$, and
the complete Forward loss enters the training loop with coefficient
$1.0$. Evaluation uses the epoch-10 checkpoint from one training run
for each task. The ten evaluation groups therefore do not estimate
training-seed variance.

\paragraph{Parameter-disjoint auxiliary head.}
The checkpoints were produced by a training implementation that also
instantiates a backward auxiliary head. This head has separate
parameters and receives detached latents. Its loss therefore does not
update the LeWM encoder, the action-conditioned predictor, or the
Forward imaginer. HAS neither queries this head nor combines its score
with the Forward cost at evaluation. We disclose it here to specify the
checkpoint provenance; all equations and reported HAS decisions use the
legacy Forward path only.

\section{Planning and evaluation protocol}
\label{app:protocol}

\paragraph{CEM configuration.}
CEM samples $300$ candidate sequences per update, retains the $30$
lowest-cost candidates, and performs $30$ distribution updates with
initial variance scale $1.0$. Default LeWM and HAS use $h{=}5$ action
blocks and receding horizon $5$, so $H{=}25$ and the controller
executes a plan of span $H$ before replanning. Long-CEM uses $h{=}10$
and receding horizon $10$, producing span $H{=}50$, while retaining
the same candidate, elite, and CEM-update counts. At $o{=}25$, this
plan extends beyond the goal time; the condition is reported for
completeness, while $o\in\{50,75,100\}$ provide the relevant
longer-horizon control.

\paragraph{Depth calculation.}
For goal offset $o$, elapsed environment steps $e$, planning span
$H{=}25$, and action-block size $b{=}5$, the implementation computes
$k=\max((o-e-H)/b,0)$. Positive remainders must be divisible by $b$;
the evaluated offsets satisfy this condition. When $k{=}0$, the Forward
imaginer is bypassed and Equation~\ref{eq:has-cost} reduces to the LeWM
terminal cost. For $o{=}100$, successive replanning steps use
\[
(e,k)\in\{(0,15),(25,10),(50,5),(75,0)\}.
\]

\paragraph{Episodes and aggregation.}
Goal offsets are $o\in\{25,50,75,100\}$ environment steps, and
the interaction budget is $2o$. Each evaluation group in
$\{42,\ldots,51\}$ provides $50$ episodes. Within a task and group,
all three planner configurations use the same starts. We first compute
one success rate per group and configuration, then report the mean and
standard deviation of these ten rates in Table~\ref{tab:main}. Paired
gaps use a group-level bootstrap with $10{,}000$ resamples.

\section{Forward depth diagnostics}
\label{app:analysis}

Figure~\ref{fig:depth} reports the mean Forward displacement and latent
norm over the ten evaluation groups. PushT displacement grows with $k$,
Reacher grows more slowly, and TwoRoom remains near $1.0$. TwoRoom
norms drop after $k{=}1$ and then stabilize; PushT and Reacher remain
in a higher-norm band. These curves are not a claim that
$F^{k}(z)\approx z_{t+kb}$. They show that the recursion used at
planning time is temporally progressive and task-dependent.
Figure~\ref{fig:latents-app} reports t-SNE of the same held-out
windows as Figure~\ref{fig:latents} and the Euclidean distances
$\|z_{t+25}-z_{t+75}\|$ versus $\|F^{10}(z_{t+25})-z_{t+75}\|$.
